sample.name: San Francisco Botanical Garden
facts: A 55-acre garden showing about 8,000 kinds of plants, opened in May 1940.
Funded by a 1927 bequest from Helene Strybing, with planting begun in 1937 using WPA funds.
A stone courtyard near the 9th Avenue entrance uses stones from Hearst's Spanish monastery.

sample.name: Billy Goat Hill
facts: Became a city park in 1975 and covers 3.5 acres.
The Beacon Trail connecting it to Walter Haas Playground opened in July 2016.

sample.name: Glen Canyon Park
facts: A 66.6-acre park centered on a forested canyon with Islais Creek running through it.
Has a 3.7-mile trail network and is a Significant Natural Resource Area.
Established in 1922

sample.name: Mission Bay Commons
facts: Spans more than two acres of lawn bookended by coastal redwoods.
San Francisco Recreation and Parks took over its management on July 1, 2023.
Address: 450 Mission Bay Blvd South, San Francisco

sample.name: Holly Park
facts: One of the city's oldest public parks.
A path around the perimeter gives views of the city from the hilltop.

sample.name: Golden Gate Heights Park
facts: Cafe owner and chicken rancher Carl Larsen donated the land that became the park.
Its playground was renovated and reopened.
Run by San Francisco Recreation & Park Department

sample.name: Immigrant Point Overlook
facts: Built in 2008 with a gift from the Sarlo Foundation of the Jewish Community Endowment Fund.
Honors those who made the journey to the United States.
Has a Woodrow Wilson quote about opening the gates to all the world engraved in stone.

sample.name: Grace Marchant Garden
facts: Created by Grace Marchant, a former Hollywood stuntwoman who moved to Telegraph Hill in 1949.
The gardens flank both sides of the Filbert Street Steps.

sample.name: George Sterling Park
facts: Named for poet George Sterling (1869-1926).
Shares its site with the Alice Marble Tennis Courts, named for the champion.
Address: 1249 Greenwich St, San Francisco

sample.name: Pioneer Park
facts: Established in 1876 on the site of the former Marine Telegraph Station.
The park surrounds Coit Tower, completed in 1933.
Established in 1876

sample.name: Crane Cove Park
facts: A waterfront park of about 7 acres next to the Pier 70 shipyard.
Plans include restoration of historic cranes and a human-powered boating facility.
Covers about 7 acres

sample.name: Huntington Park
facts: The land was donated to the city in 1915 by Arabella Huntington.
Occupies the site of the Huntington house destroyed in the 1906 earthquake and fire.
Has a replica of the Fontana delle Tartarughe fountain, installed in 1954.

sample.name: Brooks Park
facts: The hilltop has views of the Pacific Ocean, the Farallones and Mt. Tamalpais.
Has a community garden and native plant restoration.
Address: 373 Ramsell St, San Francisco

sample.name: Heron's Head Park
facts: Its EcoCenter was certified LEED Platinum by the U.S. Green Building Council in 2013.
The EcoCenter runs off the grid with solar power and a living roof.
Its Nature Exploration Area won UNICEF's 2021 Cities Inspires Award.

sample.name: Precita Park
facts: A two-acre park between Bernal Heights and Cesar Chavez Street.
Has a playground, butterfly garden, grass field and picnic areas.
Address: 3200 Folsom St, San Francisco
